title: Burn dressing
what: A nurse or doctor cleans the burned skin and puts on a special dressing. This helps the wound heal and protects it from infection.
why: For burns with blisters, burns on the face, hands, or feet, burns in children, and after first aid at an urgent care clinic.
duration: one dressing change usually takes 15 to 30 minutes; it is repeated until the burn heals
tell_doctor: When you last had a tetanus shot

prepare.title: Pain relief
prepare.text: If the dressing change hurts, ask your doctor if you can take a painkiller beforehand.

prepare.title: Clothing
prepare.text: Loose clothes that do not rub the burned area.

prepare.title: At home
prepare.text: Do not put oil, creams, or home remedies on the burn. Use only what your doctor prescribed.

bring: Products your doctor prescribed, if you were asked to bring them
steps: The old dressing is gently removed. If it is stuck, it is soaked first
The skin is rinsed with a solution
If needed, loose dead skin is removed
A healing ointment or special dressing is put on
You are told when to come for the next dressing
feel: It may hurt, especially when the old dressing comes off
Say if it hurts. They can pause or give a painkiller
After the dressing, the burning usually eases
after: Do not get the dressing wet or take it off yourself unless allowed
Do not pop blisters at home
Come for dressing changes on schedule
Once healed, protect the skin from the sun
red_flags: The wound becomes very red or swollen, smells bad, or has pus
A large burn, a burn on the face or groin, or a floppy child: call emergency services

faq.a: Not at home. The blister protects the wound. If needed, the doctor will treat it.
Shallow burns usually heal without a scar. Deep ones may leave a mark. Your doctor will tell you how to care for it.

reminders.text: Burn dressing soon. If it is painful, ask your doctor about a painkiller beforehand.
